event: Elsie wakes in the dark to the bread smell and lifts the cloth off her honey cake.
It has sunk just right in the middle, and she wraps it for the road.
Tamsin is at the bakery door at first grey light, Margery on her shoulder, bouncing on her toes.
The baker hands Tamsin a heel of warm bread through the door.
Tilly and Cora come along Thimble Canal to the bakery door, Tilly yawning, Cora with her ledger.
At the north gate Cora logs them out with the gate clerk for the E-rank troll notice.
They walk north beside the River Wend, through wet meadows full of sheep.
Elsie cuts the honey cake on a stile, and gives Cora the first slice.
Cora eats it slowly and says it is very good, and Elsie beams.
Tamsin eats two slices, and Tilly licks honey off her fingers.
Tamsin walks ahead swinging Margery, telling Tilly how to fight a troll.
Elsie walks with Cora, who says this is her first time north of the gate.
Wend Meadows' huts sit by a humped stone bridge, and the shepherds' headwoman meets them.
She says two trolls under the bridge take a sheep a night, and have since the spring floods.
She says before the floods the Wend had trout in its pools and no trolls at all.
Tilly looks at the river: the pools by the bridge are brown and shallow with silt.
Elsie asks what trolls eat when there are no sheep; the headwoman says fish, she supposes.
Under the arch two great mossy shapes lie asleep in the shallows, one big, one smaller.
Tamsin whispers that asleep is the time to hit them, and hefts Margery.
Elsie puts her hand on Margery's haft and asks Tamsin to wait; she wants to ask them first.
Tamsin looks at her a long moment, then lowers the axe to the ground.
Cora says the guild books call trolls beasts; Elsie says she'd like to hear the trolls on it.
They sit on the bank to wait for the trolls to wake, and Tilly counts the silted pools.
Tilly says the river runs too slow here, as if something upstream is holding it back.
The headwoman says an old weir stands a mile upstream, left alone since the floods.
The smaller troll wakes, sits up dripping, and stares at Tilly.
Tilly squeaks; the young troll tilts its head and squeaks back.
Tamsin stands up fast with Margery, and the big troll's eyes open.
The mother troll surges up out of the water roaring, and swings at Tamsin.
Tamsin catches the blow on Margery's haft and is thrown back into the reeds.
Elsie feels the jolt down the Tether in both her own arms.
Elsie runs in front of the young troll, arms wide, and shouts: stop, please, we came to talk.
The mother troll stops with her great fist raised, and looks down at Elsie.
Cora is at Elsie's shoulder, very white, one hand up and ready.
Elsie asks, slowly and plainly: are you hungry?
The mother troll lowers her fist and says, in a voice like stones: fish gone.
Elsie says the sheep belong to the shepherds, and asks where the fish went.
The troll points a mossy finger upstream and says: water stopped.
The young troll hides behind his mother's leg and peeks out at Elsie.
Elsie says they'll go and unstop the water, if the trolls will leave the sheep alone.
The mother troll looks at her a long, slow while, and says: yes.
Tamsin climbs out of the reeds soaked, and stares at Elsie as if she has grown wings.
Elsie checks Tamsin's arms: bruised but whole, and Tamsin laughs shakily.
Cora writes in her ledger: skills used, none; then she writes more, and keeps writing.
They walk a mile upstream along the Wend to an old stone weir.
The weir is choked with flood wrack: logs, branches and a drowned cart, jammed tight.
Above it the water stands deep and still; below it the river runs thin.
Tamsin wades in and hauls logs out one at a time, roaring with effort.
Elsie and Cora pull branches; Cora takes off her coat and rolls up her sleeves.
Cora's bandaged arm and her bare one are both mud to the elbow, and Elsie laughs.
They eat bread on the bank; Elsie rinses Cora's bandage in the river and binds it fresh.
Cora lets her, and watches the water instead of Elsie's hands.
The drowned cart stays wedged however hard Tamsin heaves.
Tilly studies the jam, chewing a singed braid, and says she can move it.
She packs a bang-flask under the cart's axle with clay and string, her hands perfectly steady.
She waves everyone back behind a willow, and Elsie holds her other hand.
The bang goes off with a crack that sends rooks up out of every tree.
The cart lurches, the wrack shifts, and the whole jam goes over the weir in a roar of water.
The Wend comes down brown and fast below, scouring the pools.
Tilly stands with her mouth open, then screams with joy and jumps into Elsie's arms.
Elsie spins her round; Tilly's face is very close to hers, and Tilly forgets to breathe.
Tamsin whoops, and Cora, very quietly, says well done to Tilly.
They walk back downstream as the water clears behind them.
By the toll bridge the pools run deeper now, and clear to the stones.
The headwoman comes to look, and shakes her head at the water.
Elsie tells her what the trolls said; the headwoman says she'll believe it at dusk.
The shepherds give them supper by the huts: mutton broth, which makes Elsie giggle.
At dusk the mother troll wades out from the arch with her son and stands in the clear pool.
Her hand flashes down, and comes up with a fat silver trout.
She gives it to her son, then looks up at Elsie on the bank and nods once.
The young troll waves a wet hand at Tilly, and Tilly waves back.
The headwoman lets out a long breath and says that's the notice done, then.
She pays them the notice by her hut door, and Elsie, Tamsin and Tilly share it.

event: She says it's too dark to walk back, and offers them her hay loft for the night.
The hay loft is warm and sweet-smelling, with one blanket for the four of them.
Cora says she will sleep by the ladder; Elsie says she'll get cold, and pulls her in.
They lie in a row in the hay: Tamsin, Elsie, Cora, and Tilly squeezed in at the end.
Tamsin's arm comes over Elsie's waist in the dark, as it did in the attic.
Elsie asks Cora what she wrote in the ledger at the bridge.
Cora is quiet a long while, then says: that the Enthraller asked a troll a question.
Elsie says she only wanted to know; Cora says she knows, and that's what she wrote.
Tilly whispers from the end that she blew up a weir on purpose, and the trout came back.
Elsie falls asleep laughing, her cheek against Cora's shoulder.
Elsie half-wakes in the dark to find Cora's hand has found hers under the blanket.
